screens.title: Optimizing System Resources with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll focus on practical techniques to make Linux servers run more effectively without automatically buying new hardware. You will learn how to measure current behavior, tune kernel parameters through sysctl, set process and service limits with ulimit and systemd, automate recurring maintenance with cron, and apply all of these changes consistently across many machines using Ansible. Start with measurement: gather baselines so you can tell if a change helps or harms. Then make small, reversible changes and measure again. We'll look at concrete examples you can practice, such as increasing the network accept queue size and raising the number of files a web server process may open. I'll also highlight common pitfalls: temporary sysctl tweaks that disappear after reboot, scripts that fail under cron because of environment differences, and changing limits without testing services. By the end you will understand not just commands, but safe operational patterns that let you tune an environment reliably and roll changes back if needed. Ready to explore the tools and the Ansible playbook that make this repeatable across a fleet?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Optimizing System Resources with Ansible
Optimizing System Resources with Ansible
Practical tuning for kernel and service behavior, scheduled maintenance, and automation at scale.
You'll learn how to: establish a baseline, change kernel parameters safely, set resource limits for users and services, schedule maintenance tasks with cron, and apply each change consistently across multiple hosts using Ansible modules. This is about predictable, auditable changes — not one-off edits.
In this lesson
  • Measure system baseline metrics before changes.
  • Tune kernel and resource limits.
  • Automate with Ansible modules for consistency.
This lesson combines command-line verification examples and Ansible playbook patterns so you can practice in a lab and later apply safely in staging and production.
Visual Summary
sysctl — kernel tunables
ulimit/systemd — resource limits
cron & Ansible — automation
Explore Key Topics
Coming up: kernel tuning examples, per-service limits with systemd, and an Ansible playbook you can run against a webserver group.
sysctl basics — view, set, persist.
ulimit & systemd — when to use each.
Ansible modules — sysctl, pam_limits, cron.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide our practice and the demo. First, you'll learn to identify opportunities for resource optimization on Linux servers. That means spotting symptoms like high run-queue times, excessive TIME_WAIT sockets, or too many open files for a service. Second, you will configure kernel parameters with sysctl so the kernel behaves better for your workload; this includes testing transient changes and making them persistent. Third, you'll control per-process and per-user resource limits by using ulimit settings and editing persistent files such as limits. conf. Fourth, you'll learn to implement cron jobs for routine maintenance such as log cleanup and scheduled performance data collection. Each objective is practical: you'll practice commands, make changes in a safe environment, and verify results. Remember the golden rule: measure, change, measure again. That principle appears throughout every objective and is key to avoiding regressions when you tune a system.

screens.title: Optimization starts with measurement
screens.narratorSegment: Optimization without measurement is guesswork. Before changing kernel tunables or resource limits, collect a baseline that captures relevant metrics for the workload you intend to improve. Examples include connection accept queues, socket states, open file counts, and process memory usage. Use simple tools and logs to build that baseline — system metrics, application logs, and previous performance captures from Chapter 8.2. A baseline gives you a control for comparison after a change. When you alter a sysctl value or increase nofile limits for a service, measure the same metrics again under comparable load. This verifies whether the change helped, made no difference, or introduced regressions. A common misconception is that increasing a limit always improves performance; it can instead expose resource starvation elsewhere or reduce stability. A practical example: you might see a backlog of connections making response times spike. Increasing net. core. somaxconn can reduce the backlog, but if the application cannot accept connections faster, you simply postpone the bottleneck. Always test in staging first and keep a rollback plan so you can quickly revert changes that harm availability. What metric will you choose as your primary success signal for a tuning change?

keyIdea.title: Measure first
keyIdea.text: Collect and compare the same metrics before and after tuning to verify real improvement and avoid destabilizing changes.

content.html:
Core Concept › Measurement Baseline
Define a measurable baseline
Select metrics tied to user experience and system reliability: connection queues, socket states, open file descriptors, CPU/memory usage, and application error rates. Record values under representative load and save them for comparison.
Example metrics: netstat or ss socket states, ulimit -n, process RSS, request latency percentiles.
Why it matters: tells you whether a change produces real user-visible improvements, not just a higher number.
Key takeaway: make one change at a time and measure the same metric you chose as your success signal.
Checklist
  • Record baseline under representative load
  • Document exact commands and config files changed
  • Test in staging before production
  • Plan a quick rollback if metrics worsen
Concrete example
If you measure many connections stuck in TIME_WAIT, you may try sysctl tuning and then re-run the same workload to compare connection setup latency and accepted connection counts.
Key Takeaway

A clear baseline and a single-variable change let you attribute effects and avoid harmful guesses.

screens.title: sysctl and kernel parameters
screens.narratorSegment: The sysctl utility exposes tunable kernel parameters that affect networking, memory management, and other kernel subsystems. You can list current values with the command that shows all parameters, and set a parameter temporarily to test its effect. For transient tests use the runtime set command which changes behavior until the next reboot. To make a change persistent across reboots you create or edit a file under the system sysctl configuration directory and then load it. An important operational detail is to use documented parameters and understand their subsystem impact. For example, increasing a network queue size affects how the kernel buffers incoming connections, which can reduce connection drops but also increase memory usage. A common mistake is to change many values at once; do single-parameter tests and measure. Also be mindful of permissions: sysctl writes require root. Use sysctl --system after updating configuration files to apply the persistent settings. Always keep documented backups of files you edit so you can restore previous behavior if a tuning change causes unexpected issues. sysctl and kernel parameters means use sysctl to read and write kernel parameters; persist changes in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply them with sysctl --system.. In practical terms, control kernel behavior at runtime and persistently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use sysctl to read and write kernel parameters; persist changes in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply them with sysctl --system.

content.html:
Definition › sysctl and Kernel Parameters
What sysctl does
sysctl exposes kernel tunables such as networking buffers and virtual memory settings. Use it to experiment safely at runtime and then persist changes you validate.
Common commands
sysctl -a
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65536
sysctl --system
Notes & example
Example parameters to consider for a busy web server are net.core.somaxconn to control the listen backlog and net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse to allow reuse of sockets in TIME_WAIT under certain conditions. Always test behavior under load and monitor memory and socket metrics after changes.
Key Takeaway

sysctl is for kernel-level tuning; use runtime edits to test and file-based configs to persist validated changes.

screens.title: Applying sysctl changes safely
screens.narratorSegment: Applying sysctl changes should follow a disciplined workflow. First, view current values to capture the baseline with a command that lists all kernel parameters. Second, apply a temporary change using the runtime write command to observe immediate effects without altering boot persistence. Third, run representative load to validate the change and monitor metrics. If the change improves behavior, create a configuration file in the system sysctl directory to make the setting persistent and then reload the system sysctl configuration. Remember to keep the file well-named and commented so reviewers understand why the change was made. A common misconception is that a runtime change alone is enough; in many environments reboots or orchestration can revert temporary tweaks. Another pitfall is applying multiple kernel changes in one step; this makes it impossible to attribute observed effects. Example: set net. core. somaxconn temporarily to a larger value, simulate connection bursts, and compare accepted connection counts and queue lengths before adding a persistent file. Make a checklist: baseline, transient test, persist, reload, verify. This reduces risk and makes the change traceable. Applying sysctl changes safely means baseline → transient test → persist via /etc/sysctl.d/ → sysctl --system → verify under load.. In practical terms, test transiently, persist thoughtfully, and reload. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Applying sysctl changes
Step-by-step
  1. Collect baseline: sysctl -a and relevant socket/file metrics.
  2. Apply temporary change: sysctl -w name=value and observe under load.
  3. If successful, create /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom-settings.conf with the parameter line.
  4. Apply persistent config: sysctl --system and re-run your tests.
  5. Document the change and keep a rollback plan.
Common mistake: changing many kernel parameters at once or skipping verification under realistic load. Always change one variable at a time and monitor the same metrics you recorded in the baseline step.
Concrete example
# temporary
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65536

# persistent file: /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom-settings.conf
net.core.somaxconn = 65536

# apply
sysctl --system

screens.title: ulimit and persistent resource limits
screens.narratorSegment: ulimit controls the maximum resources a shell or process can use, such as the number of open files, stack size, or number of processes. Running the view command shows current limits for your session so you can see whether a process will be constrained. For persistent, system-wide settings you edit the security limits configuration file or drop-in a file in the limits. d directory. For example, you can give a database user a higher file descriptor limit by adding soft and hard nofile entries for that user. A common mistake is changing ulimit only for an interactive session and assuming services adopt it; services started by systemd don’t automatically read limits. conf. For systemd-managed services, configure limits directly in the unit file. Always specify both soft and hard values when appropriate. After editing limits configuration files you should restart sessions or the affected service so the new limits take effect. If a service still shows the old limit, verify whether systemd overrides exist or whether you need to restart the process under a new PAM session. ulimit and persistent resource limits means use ulimit for session limits and /etc/security/limits.conf or limits.d for persistent per-user settings; remember services may need systemd directives instead.. In practical terms, per-user and per-process limits to protect system stability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ulimit essentials
keyIdea.text: Use ulimit for session limits and /etc/security/limits.conf or limits.d for persistent per-user settings; remember services may need systemd directives instead.

content.html:
Definition › ulimit and limits.conf
What ulimit controls
ulimit shows and sets resource limits for the current shell and child processes, including open files and process counts. Use it to protect the system from runaway processes that exhaust descriptors or memory.
Example usage
ulimit -a
ulimit -n 65536
Persisting limits
Edit /etc/security/limits.conf or add a file to /etc/security/limits.d/ with entries such as:
dbuser soft nofile 65536
dbuser hard nofile 65536
Remember that services started by systemd may not inherit these settings and should be configured at the unit level where appropriate.

screens.title: systemd unit limits vs limits.conf
screens.narratorSegment: Both limits. conf and systemd unit directives can control resource limits, but they serve different purposes and contexts. limits. conf is part of PAM-based session handling and affects login sessions and processes that inherit PAM session settings. It is useful for setting per-user limits across interactive and cron sessions. Systemd unit file directives such as the LimitNOFILE and LimitNPROC settings are applied when systemd starts a service, making them the most direct and reliable way to change limits for services. For managed services, the recommended approach is to set resource limits in the systemd unit, then reload the systemd daemon and restart the service. This prevents ambiguity about which mechanism applies. A common misconception is to edit limits. conf and assume a systemd service will pick it up; in practice services inherit systemd settings. When automating with Ansible, prefer editing or templating unit files for service-specific limits and use pam_limits for user sessions. If you need both user sessions and services adjusted, update both places and test the effective limits with su and systemctl restart as needed. systemd unit limits vs limits.conf means use systemd unit directives for services and limits.conf or pam_limits for user session limits; systemd is the authoritative path for managed services.. In practical terms, when to use per-service unit directives instead of global limits files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › systemd unit limits vs limits.conf
limits.conf / pam_limits
  • Applies to PAM sessions and interactive logins.
  • Good for user-focused settings such as developer accounts or dbuser sessions.
  • Placed in /etc/security/limits.conf or /etc/security/limits.d/.
Example entry: dbuser soft nofile 65536
systemd unit directives
  • Set per-service limits such as LimitNOFILE in the [Service] section.
  • Reload daemon and restart the service after changes.
  • Most reliable for services started by systemd.
Example: add LimitNOFILE=65536 to the unit file and run systemctl daemon-reload.
Practical advice
For services, prefer unit-level limits. Use limits.conf for user session needs. If you change both, clearly document why and test effective limits after restart.

screens.title: cron for automated maintenance
screens.narratorSegment: cron is the classic scheduler for recurring system maintenance. You can place scripts in system cron directories or schedule specific jobs with the crontab command. When writing cron jobs, always use absolute paths for commands and files because the cron environment is minimal compared to an interactive shell. Common maintenance tasks include log cleanup, database backups, and periodic performance data collection. A frequent error is forgetting that cron does not source the same environment as a user’s shell, causing scripts that run fine interactively to fail under cron. Test your scripts manually with the same minimal environment, or explicitly set needed environment variables at the top of your cron job or script. For system-wide daily tasks you can use /etc/cron. daily; for specific schedules use crontab -e for the appropriate user. When automating with Ansible, the cron module can create consistent entries across hosts. Also ensure scripts have shebang lines and executable permissions so cron can run them successfully. Finally, log cron outputs to files so you can audit runs and diagnose failures. cron for automated maintenance means use absolute paths, explicit environment variables, executable scripts with shebangs, and centralized scheduling via cron or ansible cron module.. In practical terms, scheduling reliable, environment-aware tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept › cron for automated maintenance
cron essentials
Use crontab -e for per-user jobs or /etc/cron.daily for system-wide daily tasks. Always prefer absolute paths and explicit environment settings to avoid surprises.
Example cron job
0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/cleanup_web_logs.sh >> /var/log/web_cleanup.log 2>&1

Scripts work interactively but fail under cron because they rely on user environment variables or relative paths.

keyIdea.title: Playbook pattern
keyIdea.text: Combine idempotent module tasks for kernel, limits, script deployment, and cron scheduling in a single audited playbook.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › optimize_webservers.yml walkthrough
Playbook template (annotated)
---
- name: Optimize Web Servers for Performance and Maintenance
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Set net.core.somaxconn kernel parameter
      ansible.posix.sysctl:
        name: net.core.somaxconn
        value: "65536"
        state: present
        sysctl_set: yes
        reload: yes

    - name: Increase nofile ulimit for apache user
      community.general.pam_limits:
        domain: apache
        limit_type: soft
        limit_item: nofile
        value: 65536

    - name: Increase hard nofile ulimit for apache user
      community.general.pam_limits:
        domain: apache
        limit_type: hard
        limit_item: nofile
        value: 65536

    - name: Create placeholder web log cleanup script
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        content: |
          #!/bin/bash
          echo "$(date): Running web log cleanup..." >> /var/log/web_cleanup.log
          find /var/log/httpd -type f -name "*.log-*" -mtime +7 -delete
          echo "$(date): Web log cleanup completed." >> /var/log/web_cleanup.log
        dest: /usr/local/bin/cleanup_web_logs.sh
        mode: '0755'

    - name: Schedule daily web log cleanup cron job
      ansible.builtin.cron:
        name: "Daily web log cleanup"
        minute: "0"
        hour: "3"
        job: "/usr/local/bin/cleanup_web_logs.sh"
        user: root
        state: present
Follow the playbook with verification steps: sysctl query, limits file inspection, script permission check, and crontab listing. Keep the playbook in version control and test it with ansible-playbook against a staging inventory first.

screens.title: Testing, verification, and rollback
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and verification are essential parts of any optimization workflow. After applying a change manually or via Ansible, run the same checks you used to produce the baseline. For kernel parameters use the sysctl query, for ulimit check interactive sessions or inspect limits configuration, and for systemd unit changes confirm the running service’s effective limits after a restart. Automate verification tasks as follow-up Ansible tasks when possible to produce machine-readable pass/fail outputs. In addition to verification, maintain a rollback plan that includes the original configuration, a playbook to restore it, and a schedule for performing the rollback if metrics indicate regression. Common misconceptions include assuming a quick reboot will restore service health; sometimes a rolling rollback or targeted configuration revert is safer. Also document who approves changes and keep playbooks in version control with meaningful commit messages. A concrete example: after increasing net. core. somaxconn and restarting your web process, re-run a load test and compare connection backlog and response percentiles. If response percentiles worsen, revert the sysctl file and reload sysctl configuration. In practical terms, validate every change and have a fallback plan. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll focus on practical techniques to make Linux servers run more effectively without automatically buying new hardware. You will learn how to measure current behavior, tune kernel parameters through sysctl, set process and service limits with ulimit and systemd, automate recurring maintenance with cron, and apply all of these changes consistently across many machines using Ansible. Start with measurement: gather baselines so you can tell if a change helps or harms. Then make small, reversible changes and measure again. We'll look at concrete examples you can practice, such as increasing the network accept queue size and raising the number of files a web server process may open. I'll also highlight common pitfalls: temporary sysctl tweaks that disappear after reboot, scripts that fail under cron because of environment differences, and changing limits without testing services. By the end you will understand not just commands, but safe operational patterns that let you tune an environment reliably and roll changes back if needed. Ready to explore the tools and the Ansible playbook that make this repeatable across a fleet?

These objectives will guide our practice and the demo. First, you'll learn to identify opportunities for resource optimization on Linux servers. That means spotting symptoms like high run-queue times, excessive TIME_WAIT sockets, or too many open files for a service. Second, you will configure kernel parameters with sysctl so the kernel behaves better for your workload; this includes testing transient changes and making them persistent. Third, you'll control per-process and per-user resource limits by using ulimit settings and editing persistent files such as limits. conf. Fourth, you'll learn to implement cron jobs for routine maintenance such as log cleanup and scheduled performance data collection. Each objective is practical: you'll practice commands, make changes in a safe environment, and verify results. Remember the golden rule: measure, change, measure again. That principle appears throughout every objective and is key to avoiding regressions when you tune a system.

Beyond hands-on commands, we emphasise automation and safety. First, you will automate settings across multiple hosts using Ansible so changes are consistent, auditable, and reversible. Second, you'll practise the golden rule of optimization: measure, change, measure again. That technique prevents false assumptions about improvements. Third, you'll learn to test changes in staging before production and how to roll back if they cause regressions. These are operational competencies: automation reduces human error, baselines make outcomes measurable, and testing protects availability. Throughout the lesson you'll see Ansible examples that apply sysctl, pam_limits, cron scheduling, and systemd edits. Practicing these tasks in a lab lets you build confidence and also creates artifacts you can review during change control or audits. Learning Objectives — Continued means automate with ansible, measure and validate changes, and use staging and rollback practices for safe deployment.. In practical terms, automation, verification, and safe deployment practices. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Optimization without measurement is guesswork. Before changing kernel tunables or resource limits, collect a baseline that captures relevant metrics for the workload you intend to improve. Examples include connection accept queues, socket states, open file counts, and process memory usage. Use simple tools and logs to build that baseline — system metrics, application logs, and previous performance captures from Chapter 8.2. A baseline gives you a control for comparison after a change. When you alter a sysctl value or increase nofile limits for a service, measure the same metrics again under comparable load. This verifies whether the change helped, made no difference, or introduced regressions. A common misconception is that increasing a limit always improves performance; it can instead expose resource starvation elsewhere or reduce stability. A practical example: you might see a backlog of connections making response times spike. Increasing net. core. somaxconn can reduce the backlog, but if the application cannot accept connections faster, you simply postpone the bottleneck. Always test in staging first and keep a rollback plan so you can quickly revert changes that harm availability. What metric will you choose as your primary success signal for a tuning change?

The sysctl utility exposes tunable kernel parameters that affect networking, memory management, and other kernel subsystems. You can list current values with the command that shows all parameters, and set a parameter temporarily to test its effect. For transient tests use the runtime set command which changes behavior until the next reboot. To make a change persistent across reboots you create or edit a file under the system sysctl configuration directory and then load it. An important operational detail is to use documented parameters and understand their subsystem impact. For example, increasing a network queue size affects how the kernel buffers incoming connections, which can reduce connection drops but also increase memory usage. A common mistake is to change many values at once; do single-parameter tests and measure. Also be mindful of permissions: sysctl writes require root. Use sysctl --system after updating configuration files to apply the persistent settings. Always keep documented backups of files you edit so you can restore previous behavior if a tuning change causes unexpected issues. sysctl and kernel parameters means use sysctl to read and write kernel parameters; persist changes in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply them with sysctl --system.. In practical terms, control kernel behavior at runtime and persistently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Applying sysctl changes should follow a disciplined workflow. First, view current values to capture the baseline with a command that lists all kernel parameters. Second, apply a temporary change using the runtime write command to observe immediate effects without altering boot persistence.
